result:
There's a particular ache in old photographs. Not nostalgia exactly—something stranger. Look at any photograph from decades ago and you're looking at people who were, at the moment the shutter clicked, exactly as real as you are now. Someone was mid-sentence. Someone had an itch on their ankle. Someone was worried about a conversation they'd have tomorrow, which is now a century past.

We know this intellectually, but photographs make it felt. The woman squinting into the sun in 1923 had a whole interior weather system—private jokes, grudges, songs stuck in her head. The gap-toothed boy holding the fish he was clearly proud of spent that entire day being alive, and it culminated in that moment, and he couldn't have known a stranger would someday study his face.

Photographs flatten time in a way nothing else does. A portrait of a soldier from 1917 doesn't show you a dead man; it shows you a person who didn't yet know what the next year held. That asymmetry—our knowledge of their future, their ignorance of it—is almost unbearable. We watch them like we'd watch characters in a film we've already seen the ending of.

Maybe that's why we keep them. Not to remember, exactly, but to testify. Someone was here. They loved things. They squinted into the sun. The proof is grainy and faded, but it insists: this happened. This person was as vivid and unrepeatable as you feel yourself to be, right now, reading this.
